Estonia
es-TOH-nee-a
n. (the northern Baltic province whose German masters took the Reformation in 1524 and whose Estonian Bible came only in 1739)
Latin Estonia, from the Aestii named by Tacitus; Estonian Eesti, a Finnic tongue unrelated to the German of its rulers.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Estonia is the Baltic province where the Reformation arrived quickly for the rulers and slowly for the people. Reval and Dorpat, German Hanseatic towns under the Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order, had evangelical preaching by 1523 and 1524, iconoclastic riots followed, and the town councils carried the Reformation through within a few years; a Lutheran establishment was in place while the Estonian-speaking peasantry remained serfs of German landlords who had no particular interest in teaching them. The gap between the two was closed slowly and by individual labour. Heinrich Stahl published an Estonian handbook and sermon collection from 1632, Anton thor Helle produced the first complete Estonian Bible in 1739, and the decisive change came through the Moravians, whose Estonian-speaking lay preachers from the 1730s reached the peasantry as the established church had not in two centuries. Balthasar Russow, himself of Estonian descent, wrote the chronicle of Livonia in German and recorded the peasants' condition with a candour his class did not share. The dictionary enters Estonia because it shows a Reformation complete in law and two hundred years late in the language of the people, and because the lesson is that a confession in a ruler's tongue converts the ruler.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a serf as a servile tenant attached to the soil; a chronicle as a historical account of facts in order of time; a vassal as one who holds land of a superior; and a handbook as a manual.

expand to see more

SERF, n. A servant or slave employed in husbandry, and in some countries attached to the soil, and transferred with it.

CHRONICLE, n. An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.

VASSAL, n. A feudatory; a tenant; one who holds land of a superior and vows fidelity and homage to him.

MANUAL, n. A small book, such as may be carried in the hand or conveniently handled.

PEASANTRY, n. Peasants; rustics; the body of countrymen, or tillers of the earth.

Key Scripture

1Co 14:9 — "So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air."

Act 2:8 — "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?"

Rom 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

Jam 2:1 — "My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons."

Modern Corruption

Northern Baltic province whose German towns reformed by 1524 while the Estonian peasantry waited until 1739 for a complete Bible in their own tongue.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the respect of persons that lets a church be thorough for its gentry and negligent for its serfs. Estonia's Lutheran establishment was settled, catechised and preached to in German within a decade; the people who worked the land got an Estonian Bible two hundred and fifteen years later. The apostle's prohibition is exact and was ignored: “have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons” (Jam 2:1). A ministry that will not learn the language of the poor has made that choice whatever it professes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that preaching must reach the hearer in his own speech, or it is not preaching to him. “how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9) is the question Estonian peasants could have asked of a German sermon for two centuries, and the Pentecostal gift was given to answer it, that men hear “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8). The chain of necessity runs back to the sender, for “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14), and the Moravian lay preachers of the 1730s were the first to go.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek glossa (G1100), a tongue; Greek prosopolepsia (G4382), respect of persons; Greek dialektos (G1258), the speech of a region.

expand to see more

Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue, and so a language; “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood”, 1 Corinthians 14:9.

Greek prosopolepsia (G4382) — respect of persons, partiality; “with respect of persons”, James 2:1.

Greek dialektos (G1258) — the speech of a region; “in our own tongue, wherein we were born”, Acts 2:8.

Greek akouo (G191) — to hear, to hearken; “how shall they hear without a preacher?”, Romans 10:14.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; “And how shall they preach, except they be sent?”, Romans 10:15.

Usage

"“with respect of persons” (Jam 2:1) — a German establishment and an Estonian-speaking serfdom."

"“in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8) — the complete Estonian Bible of 1739."

"“how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — Moravian lay preachers from the 1730s."
